newsitem.title: GERMANY: Regional talks see progress in German sick pay row.
newsitem.headline: Regional talks see progress in German sick pay row.

text.p: German trade union officials said on Monday they had made some progress in talks with engineering employers in the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg aimed at finding a solution to the dispute on sick pay cuts.

The region, home to Daimler-Benz AG's Mercedes car-making unit, has been one of the main focuses of nationwide protests against a new law cutting sick pay allowances from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

Walter Riester, vice-chairman of the IG Metall trade union, said during a break in the talks that there was a "strong chance" for agreement on employment protection measures that the union wants included in new regional contract agreements.

Job protection measures formed the main part of IG Metall's 1997 wage demand announced earlier this month. Agreement on such measures could pave the way for a possible compromise on sick pay, which was due to be discussed on Monday afternoon.

Union officials had said before the regional talks -- the first since national-level discussions collpased last week -- that they were ready to use strike action to defend sick pay, which employers want to cut as part overall labour cost reductions.

"We don't want to take industrial action but we will not back down from it if no solution is found on the negotiating table," Walter Riester, vice-chairman of the IG Metall trade union told German radio.
Around 800,000 of the metal and engineering sector's 3.5 million workers are employed in Baden-Wuerttemberg.

Dieter Hundt, chief negotiator for the employers' side, said they would be ready to make compromises if IG Metall changed its position. The union has so far insisted that sick pay must continue to be paid at 100 percent of salary.
Some 2,000 people protested outside the building in Freudenstadt where the talks went ahead, accusing employers of breach of contract by seeking to introduce the cuts.
Baden-Wuerttenberg along with the North-Rhine Westphalia steel-making region were the two areas worst hit by walk-outs involving hundreds of thousands of workers last week.

An earlier day of protest by workers this month forced major companies including Daimler to postpone plans to implement the cuts until wider agreement on wages and labour costs had been reached with the union.
IG Metall and Gesamtmetall had met for two days of talks to attempt to resolve the dispute last week but talks broke down with both sides accusing the other of intransigence.
Gesamtmetall said after the collapse of discussions that issues such as sick pay would now most likely have to be solved on the regional level.
